name: FP64 (binary64, double)
notes: Default precision in scientific computing and LAPACK. GeForce GPUs run it at 1/32 to 1/64 of their FP32 rate; data-centre GPUs such as A100 and H100 run it at 1/2.

name: FP32 (binary32, single)
notes: The usual accumulator for tensor-core matrix multiplies on FP16, BF16 and FP8 inputs, and the format of master weights in mixed-precision training.

name: TF32 (TensorFloat-32)
notes: TF32 is a compute mode, not a storage format: tensors stay FP32 in memory, and the tensor cores round inputs to a 10-bit mantissa (19 meaningful bits) and accumulate in FP32. It has FP32's range with FP16's precision.

name: BF16 (bfloat16)
notes: It is the top 16 bits of an FP32 value: the same 8-bit exponent and range, but only about 2 to 3 significant decimal digits. FP16 training needs loss scaling; BF16 training does not. Some hardware flushes BF16 subnormals to zero.
standard: Google Brain; no IEEE standard (de facto)

name: FP16 (binary16, half)
notes: Largest finite value is 65504, so gradients overflow or underflow without loss scaling. This was the input format of the first tensor cores (Volta).

name: FP8 E4M3 (OCP)
notes: There is no infinity. The single NaN pattern is S.1111.111, which frees the other all-ones-exponent codes for finite values, so the maximum is 1.75 x 2^8 = 448. Used for weights and activations. (Graphcore/AMD MI300 'FNUZ' E4M3 uses bias 8, max 240 and a single NaN at -0; it is a different encoding.)

name: FP8 E5M2 (OCP)
notes: Behaves like IEEE: it has infinities and NaNs, and the same exponent range as FP16. More range and less precision than E4M3, so it is typically used for gradients.

name: FP6 E3M2 (OCP MX)
notes: No infinity and no NaN: every code is a finite number. The maximum is 1.75 x 2^4 = 28. In MX it is used as an MXFP6 element under an E8M0 block scale.

name: FP6 E2M3 (OCP MX)
notes: No infinity and no NaN. The maximum is 1.875 x 2^2 = 7.5. More precision and less range than E3M2.

name: FP4 E2M1 (OCP MX)
notes: Only 16 codes. The magnitudes are 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4 and 6; there is no infinity or NaN. It is only useful with a block scale.

name: E8M0 scale (OCP MX)
notes: An unsigned power-of-two scale, 2^(E-127). 0xFF is NaN and there is no zero. It is the shared scale in every MX format.

name: MXFP4
notes: Each block of 32 E2M1 elements shares one 8-bit E8M0 power-of-two scale, so storage is (32x4 + 8)/32 = 4.25 bits per element. The value is scale x element. The spec suggests choosing the scale as floor(log2(amax)) minus the element format's emax (2 for E2M1). Other MX members: MXFP8 (E4M3 or E5M2), MXFP6 (E3M2 or E2M3) and MXINT8.

name: NVFP4
scaleFormat: fp8-e4m3 per block + fp32 per tensor
notes: Each block of 16 E2M1 values has an FP8 E4M3 scale (fractional, not just a power of two), and a second FP32 scale applies to the whole tensor: x = e2m1 x s_block(E4M3) x s_tensor(FP32). Storage is (16x4 + 8)/16 = 4.5 bits per element plus the per-tensor scale. Within a block the range is 6 x 448 = 2688 before the tensor scale. Supported natively by Blackwell tensor cores.

name: INT8
notes: A two's-complement integer from -128 to 127. Symmetric quantisation usually uses -127 to 127 with a scale (and, for asymmetric schemes, a zero point). Products are accumulated in INT32. TPU v1 used it for inference, as do most NPUs. Here 'mantissa' means the 7 magnitude bits, and minNormal holds the minimum integer.

name: INT4
notes: A two's-complement integer from -8 to 7, with two values packed per byte. Mostly used for weight-only LLM quantisation (GPTQ, AWQ, llama.cpp Q4) with a per-group scale, often per 32 to 128 weights. Here 'mantissa' means the 3 magnitude bits, and minNormal holds the minimum integer.
